'''''Euphorbia flanaganii''''', commonly known as '''Transkei medusa's head''', is a [[succulent]] plant that belongs to the family [[Euphorbiaceae]]. It is endemic to [[South Africa]].<ref name = powo/> Due to the breadth of the Euphorbiaceae, little research specific to ''E. flanaganii'' has been conducted. 

==Taxonomy==
It is believed to be closely related to ''E. hypogaea'' and ''E. procumbens'', resulting from a common [[speciation]] event. However, the [[phylogenetic]] association between the three species remains relatively unreliable, with values of only 53/.66 attributed to the linkage.<ref name="peirson">{{cite journal | last1=Peirson | first1=Jess A. | last2=Bruyns | first2=Peter V. | last3=Riina | first3=Ricarda | last4=Morawetz | first4=Jeffery J. | last5=Berry | first5=Paul E. | year=2013 | title=A molecular phylogeny and classification of the largely succulent and mainly African Euphorbia subg. Athymalus (Euphorbiaceae) | journal=Taxon | volume=62 | issue=6 | pages=1178–1199 | doi=10.12705/626.12}}</ref> ''Euphorbia flanaganii'' is in subgenus Athymalus,<ref name="peirson" /><ref name="bruyns2006">{{cite journal | last1=Bruyns | first1=P.V. | last2=Mapaya | first2=R.J. | last3=Hedderson | first3=T. | year=2006 | title=A new subgeneric classification for Euphorbia (Euphorbiaceae) in [[southern Africa]] based on ITS and psbA-trnH sequence data. | journal=Taxon | volume=55 | issue=2 | pages=397–420 | doi=10.2307/25065587| jstor=25065587 }}</ref> which comprises 150 species.

==Description==
[[File:Euphorbia_flanaganii_1.jpg|thumb|left|Inflorescence]]
It is an agglomerated, [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|thorn]]y, succulent plant with snake-like branches that has a swollen underground stem. It is a dwarf shrub with a size of 0.02 to 0.05 m in height that is found at an altitude of 30 to 185 meters. Leaves are rather small, only 10 mm long and 1 mm broad. Its branches grow horizontally, up to 400 mm in diameter. It has inflorescence in [[cyathium]] with a single, 4 mm long flower per flower stalk that bloom in late summer and autumn.<ref>Williams, V.L et al. 2014. Euphorbia flanaganii N.E.Br. National Assessment: Red List of South African Plants version 2017.1. Accessed on 2019/02/11.</ref>

It has photosynthetic [[Aerial stem modification|modified stems]] that lack, or have delayed development of, [[periderm]].<ref name="bruyns2011" /> Careful observation of ''E. flanaganii'' specimens also reveals modified, needle-like leaves, radial geometric symmetry, and a seemingly tuberous above ground root structure.

==Distribution==
''Euphorbia flanaganii'' is native to the east-central and southeastern [[Cape Provinces]] and southern [[KwaZulu-Natal]] in [[South Africa]].<ref name = powo/>

==Evolution==
Species within subgenus ''Athymalus'', including ''E. flanaganii'', are found only in arid regions such as the [[Arabian Peninsula]], the [[Canary Islands]], [[Madagascar]], and [[South Africa]].<ref name="peirson" /><ref name="bruyns2011">{{cite journal | last1=Bruyns | first1=P.V. | last2=Klak | first2=C. | last3=Hanáček | first3=P. | year=2011 | title=Age and diversity in Old World succulent species of Euphorbia (Euphorbiaceae). | journal=Taxon | volume=60 | issue=6 | pages=1717–1733| doi=10.1002/tax.606016 }}</ref> The historical and modern day geographical home of the subgenus, and the diversity level among species in the same region, suggest species in ''Athymalus'' are a lineage of early [[divergence]].<ref name="peirson" /><ref name="bruyns2006" /> A large speciation event of ''Euphorbia'' is believed to have occurred over the course of 3 million to 10 million years ago, due to a significant [[climate change|change in climate]], in what are now considered to be modern arid regions; the Athymalus subgenus is believed to have evolved during this period.<ref name="peirson" /><ref name="bruyns2011" /><ref>{{cite book | last1=Partridge | first1=T.C. | last2=Maud | first2=R.R. | year=2000 | title=The Cenozoic of southern Africa. | location=Oxford | publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> 

Given the present body of knowledge that pertains to other Euphorbia species found in the same regions as ''E. flanaganii'', and historical evolutionary events, it is highly likely that ''E. flanaganii'' is roughly 3–10 million years old as well.<ref name="bruyns2011" />
